uncited: Dual Contouring and Surface Nets are isosurface extraction algorithms that generate a single vertex per active grid cell (voxel) rather than placing vertices on cell edges like Marching Cubes [S1, S2, S3, unofficial].
This family prioritizes mesh sparsity and feature preservation over topological simplicity, producing watertight meshes with fewer triangles [S5, S9, S1, unofficial].

Dual Contouring optimizes vertex position via a Quadratic Error Function (QEF) to preserve sharp features, while Surface Nets uses a weighted average of intersection points for a faster, normal-free approximation [S1, S2, S3, unofficial].
All methods in this family operate on a regular 3D grid where each cell is evaluated against an isovalue $I$.
A cell is "active" if the scalar field values at its vertices straddle the isosurface.
Unlike Marching Cubes, which may produce multiple vertices per cell, these methods produce exactly one vertex per active cell [S1, S2, S3, unofficial].
**Cell Traversal**: Iterating over all cells $(x, y, z)$ and determining intersection status via vertex signs relative to $I$.
**Vertex Placement**: Computing a single 3D position $V$ for each active cell.
*   In **Dual Contouring**, $V$ minimizes the error $\|AV - b\|^2$, where rows of $A$ are surface normals and $b_i = n_i \cdot P_i$ [S1, unofficial].
*   In **Surface Nets**, $V$ is the centroid of intersection points on the cell edges [S1, unofficial].
**Topology Construction**: Connecting the single vertex of each active cell to form the mesh.
This typically involves identifying shared edges between cells and forming quads or triangles from the vertices of the adjacent cells [S5, S1, unofficial].
Dual Contouring was introduced by Yu [S1, S2, unofficial] as an improvement over Marching Cubes to handle sharp features and non-manifold geometries.
Surface Nets was proposed by Kruger et al. [S1, unofficial] as a simplified alternative to Dual Contouring that avoids the computational cost of QEF solving.
Sparse Dual Marching Cubes extends these concepts to sparse voxel representations [unofficial].
These methods are widely used in real-time rendering and geometric modeling where mesh quality and sparsity are balanced [S5, S9, S1, unofficial].
